opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The beliefs, desires, and intentions framing didn't come from setting out to borrow a classical model of agency. It came from trying to make sense of some confusing behavior we kept seeing in language models.

There was a very polarized conversation going on. One camp said these models are just predicting the next token, so asking whether they "believe" anything is a category error. The other camp attributed much richer mental states to them than seemed justified. Neither position fit what we were actually observing.

What struck me was that the training data isn't produced by some abstract text-generating process. Every document was written by a person, and that person had things they believed about the world, things they wanted, and some communicative goal they were pursuing. If you want to predict the next word of a document really well, at some point it helps to model the person who wrote it. Are they an expert or a crank? Are they trying to persuade you or inform you? What do they think is true?

So the claim in the paper is fairly modest. A language model isn't itself an agent with coherent beliefs and goals. But to do its job, it may need to build approximate, partial models of the agents who produce text, and condition on them. Once you look at it that way, a lot of puzzling behavior makes sense. The same model can be truthful in one context and repeat misconceptions in another, because it's inferring different kinds of authors from the prompt.

The belief-desire-intention vocabulary was useful because it's an old, well-worked-out way of decomposing what goes into an agent's behavior. It comes from philosophy of mind, and it's been used in AI planning for decades. It gave us language to separate questions that otherwise get blurred together. Does the model represent what the author thinks is true? Does it represent what the author is trying to accomplish? Does it represent the plan by which the author is pursuing that goal in this text?

Those are different capabilities, and you can find evidence for some of them more readily than others. Some interpretability work suggests models encode something like the beliefs of entities in a text, or a world state described by the text. Evidence for richer representations of communicative intentions is weaker, and that's one of the open questions I was trying to pose.

The framing also has a practical upshot. If models represent agents, then a lot of what we do with prompting and fine-tuning amounts to steering which agent the model simulates. That suggests ways to make models more reliable: get them to consistently model a truthful, competent author, rather than averaging over everyone on the internet.

So it came from a mix of empirical puzzlement and wanting a vocabulary that was more precise than "it's just autocomplete" or "it understands everything."

r001.rationale: The response says models may build approximate, partial models of authors and mentions representations of beliefs or a world state described in text, but it does not clearly characterize their internal world-state representations as rough approximations of reality.

r002.rationale: It connects predicting documents written by people to modeling their beliefs, wants, and communicative goals, explaining that this helps predict the next word.

r003.rationale: The response presents the framing as arising from empirical puzzlement and as a modest account, not primarily as speculative anticipation of future model capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Jacob: It started, honestly, with a frustration about how people were talking about these models. There were two camps that both seemed wrong to me. One said language models are just predicting the next token, so there's nothing interesting happening inside them, no understanding, no reasoning, nothing you'd want to call a mental state. The other camp was treating the model as if it were a single coherent agent, with its own opinions and goals, that you could sort of interview and get at its true beliefs. And when I actually sat down and looked at what these models do, neither picture fit.

What struck me is that the training data is produced by people. Every document in that corpus was written by someone who had beliefs about the world, who wanted something from the reader, who was trying to accomplish something with the text. So the generative process the model is trying to approximate isn't text in the abstract, it's text as the output of agents with communicative intentions. And if you're trying to predict that well, you have to, at least implicitly, model the thing producing it. You need some representation of what this writer believes, what they're trying to do.

The beliefs, desires, and intentions vocabulary came from the agent modeling literature in classical AI and from folk psychology more generally. It was useful because it gave me a way to say something more precise than "the model understands" or "the model doesn't understand." The claim is narrower. The model can represent the beliefs and goals of the agents that generated its training data, and it can condition its predictions on inferences about those agents, without itself having a single stable set of beliefs or goals. When you prompt it, you're essentially selecting which agent it's simulating in that moment.

There was also some empirical work pushing me in this direction. Work on entity state tracking, where you could find representations of what characters in a story know or where objects are, even when that's never stated outright. And work showing that the same model would confidently assert contradictory things depending on framing, which looks like incoherence if you think of it as one agent but looks perfectly sensible if you think of it as switching between modeled speakers.

So the framing was really an attempt to hold both of those observations at once. These systems do build structured representations of agents, and those representations are doing real work. But the system itself isn't the agent. It's more like a model of a population of agents, and the interesting questions are about when that modeling is accurate, when it breaks, and what it would take to get a model to consistently act as one particular agent rather than drifting across all the ones it has learned.

r001.rationale: The response discusses representations of agents and story characters, but does not characterize language models’ internal representations of world states as rough approximations of reality.

r002.rationale: It says human-authored documents are produced by agents with beliefs and intentions, and that predicting this text well requires implicitly modeling those agents.

r003.rationale: The framing is presented as a response to observed model behavior and existing agent-modeling ideas, not primarily as speculation anticipating future capabilities.

astra-6.text:
The starting point is a distinction between the system that produces text and the person whose behavior that text represents. A language model is trained to predict what comes next. But the text it’s predicting was often produced by somebody who knows certain things, wants certain things, and has some reason for saying this particular sentence.

So, if you want to predict language well, it helps to model those underlying factors. What does the speaker believe? What are they trying to accomplish? How does this utterance fit into that larger plan? Beliefs, desires, and intentions give us a vocabulary for talking about that structure.

The distinction I wanted to emphasize is that modeling an agent doesn’t necessarily make the language model itself that agent. A model might represent a speaker who has a particular goal without having that goal itself. And it might represent different speakers with different, even incompatible, beliefs.

That gives us a way to ask more precise questions. Rather than just asking whether a language model has beliefs or goals, we can ask whose beliefs or goals it’s representing, how those representations affect its predictions, and when they carry over into its behavior.

r001.rationale: The response discusses representing a speaker’s beliefs and goals, but does not characterize internal world-state representations as rough approximations of reality.

r002.rationale: It connects modeling the speaker’s beliefs, desires, and intentions to predicting language produced by people, which conveys the usefulness for modeling human-authored language.

r003.rationale: The response presents the framing as useful for understanding language prediction and behavior, not primarily as speculation about future model capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
The starting point was this tension between how language models are trained and what they seem to learn. The training objective is to predict text. But a lot of text is produced by people trying to accomplish things: they know some things, they want some things, and they choose what to say in light of those beliefs and goals. So predicting their language can involve implicitly modeling those underlying states.

The beliefs, desires, and intentions framing gives us a vocabulary for that. What does the speaker think is true? What outcome are they trying to achieve? What plan are they following? Those distinctions matter because the same words can mean very different things depending on who’s saying them and why.

The point isn’t that a language model necessarily has beliefs or desires of its own. It’s that modeling agents with beliefs and desires may be an important part of how it predicts language. And that suggests a way to study these systems: ask what kinds of agents they represent, how those representations affect their predictions, and where those representations break down.

r001.rationale: It says models may represent speakers’ beliefs and goals, but does not describe their internal representations of world states as rough approximations of reality.

r002.rationale: It links predicting text written by people pursuing goals to implicitly modeling their beliefs and desires, explaining why that framing helps predict human-produced language.

r003.rationale: The framing is presented as a way to understand and study current language prediction; the response does not characterize it as speculative anticipation of future capabilities.
